title: The gifts come up
hook: bread and wine are carried forward; a drop of water mingles with the wine

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nicene Creed, then the prayers of the faithful. Your line was we believe, then we ask.

The prayers for the world end, and the whole feel of the Mass shifts. People sit. Baskets move down the rows: the rustle of envelopes, a kid proudly dropping in a coin. Up front, servers lay a white cloth on the altar and set down a cup and a book. Then, from the back of the church, a few ordinary people walk up the aisle, a couple maybe, or a family with a nervous child, carrying a plate of bread and a small glass jug of wine. They hand them to the priest and sit back down. It looks like nothing.
screen: `BASKETS DOWN THE ROWS.` → `A FAMILY WALKS UP THE AISLE.` → `BREAD AND WINE, HANDED OVER.`

segments.voice: Offertory comes from the Latin offerre, to bring forward, to offer. The Mass has two great halves. The first is the word: readings, homily, creed, prayers. The second, starting now, is the Eucharist, the meal. And it starts with ordinary people carrying up ordinary things. Bread, which the earth gave and human hands made. Wine, the same. In the early Church, people often brought bread and wine from their own homes, and the leftovers went to the poor. The collection is the same idea: the people's gifts, for the Church and the poor, carried up with the bread. Then the priest lifts the bread a little and blesses God for it, in a prayer shaped like something much older. It echoes the Jewish blessings said over bread and wine at the table, the ones that begin baruch atah, blessed are you, the kind Jesus himself would have said. The priest or deacon pours the wine into the chalice, then adds a single drop of water. He says a short prayer under his breath, borrowed from an ancient Christmas prayer: it asks that, since Christ came to share our humanity, we might come to share his divinity. The water disappears into the wine, and it can't be taken back out. Catholics see in it the human joined to the divine, and some see the water and blood from Christ's side on the cross. Then the priest washes his hands. From mercy and glory through the creed, this week the word was given. Now the ordinary things go up.
screen: `OFFERRE: TO BRING FORWARD.` · `ORDINARY PEOPLE, ORDINARY BREAD.` · `A BLESSING OLDER THAN THE MASS.` · `ONE DROP OF WATER IN THE WINE.` · then: `THE ORDINARY, CARRIED UP.`

segments.voice: Think of one ordinary piece of your day: the commute, a sink of dishes, the kids' bedtime. Picture carrying it forward in your hands, like that family in the aisle, and setting it down. If you pray, offer it to God, like a drop in the wine; if you don't, simply let it count, as part of something larger.
Offertory. The bringing forward of bread and wine, and the people's gifts, at the start of the Eucharist. Today's word.
Your line: the ordinary is carried up. Bread, wine, a coin in the basket. Day one hundred and twelve, in the books.

chat.says: Why do people carry bread and wine up the aisle at Mass?
options: Ordinary gifts from the people begin the Eucharist, carried up with the collection.
It's the priest's own bread, brought up by helpers so he can stay put.
Only bread baked at home can be used, so families take turns bringing it.
chat.meaning: The second half of Mass starts with ordinary people carrying up ordinary things: bread and wine, with the people's gifts.

notes: Prayers at the preparation of the gifts are paraphrased (the ICEL 2011 wording is copyrighted). 'Blessed are you, Lord God of all creation' is spoken without quotation marks as a description; a Keeper should confirm this is acceptable or ask for further paraphrase.
The water-and-wine prayer derives from an ancient Christmas collect (attributed to the Leonine/Verona sacramentary); confirm the trapdoor's phrasing.
Early Christians bringing bread and wine from home, and leftovers given to the poor: commonly stated; confirm.
The Jewish berakhah comparison (Baruch atah Adonai …) is offered respectfully as a shared root, not a comparison; confirm.

No Douay-Rheims quotation used today (Psalm 25:6, 'I will wash my hands among the innocent', considered and left out).
